1.text:
What Can Starlight Tell Us?

In Deck 14 we studied the Sun, the one star close enough to examine up close. Now we turn to the billions of stars we can only see as tiny points of light. We will never visit them. We can't scoop up a sample. So how do astronomers know anything at all?

The answer is in the light. Almost everything we know about stars comes from it. This deck asks one big question: what can starlight tell us about a star? By the end, you'll be able to read a star's temperature, speed, distance, ingredients, and even its mass, all from light.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can rate yourself at the end.

I can describe the electromagnetic spectrum and use c = λ × f. I can tell continuous, emission and absorption spectra apart. I can identify elements from their spectral fingerprints. I can explain redshift and blueshift, the Doppler effect. I can use a star's color to find its temperature.

I can compare telescopes by light gathering and resolution. I can explain atmospheric windows and why Hubble and Webb fly in space. I can find distance by parallax and tell brightness from luminosity. I can classify stars OBAFGKM and build the H-R diagram. And I can find star masses from binaries and link mass to lifespan. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.1, ES.1.4 and ES.1.2, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum is the whole range of light, from long radio waves to short gamma rays. Visible light, the rainbow your eyes can see, is only a thin slice in the middle.

Here are the bands from longest to shortest wavelength. Radio waves are over 1 m long. Microwaves run from 1 mm to 1 m. Infrared spans 1 µm to 1 mm. Visible light is just 400 to 700 nm. Ultraviolet goes from 20 to 400 nm, X-rays from 0.01 to 20 nm, and gamma rays are under 0.01 nm.

The rule to remember: longer waves carry lower energy, and shorter waves carry higher energy. That's why UV can sunburn you and X-rays can pass through skin, but radio waves pass harmlessly through you all day.

Did you know? A radio wave can be longer than a school bus, while a gamma ray is far smaller than an atom.

4.text:
All Light, One Speed

Every kind of light travels at the same speed in empty space: about 300,000 km/s. Radio or gamma, red or blue, they all move at c.

Waves follow one simple rule: c = λ × f. Here λ (lambda) is the wavelength, the distance from crest to crest. And f is the frequency, how many waves pass each second, measured in hertz (Hz).

Since c can't change, the two must trade off. A long wave has a low frequency. A short wave has a high frequency. Picture two people walking side by side at the same speed, one with long strides and one with short quick steps. The short-stepper takes many more steps per second.

Did you know? At 300,000 km/s, light could circle Earth about 7 times in one second.

5.text:
Three Kinds of Spectra

Spread light into its colors and you get a spectrum. There are three kinds, and each one tells a different story.

A continuous spectrum shows every color, a smooth rainbow. It comes from a hot, dense glow, like a glowing light bulb filament or the inside of a star. An emission spectrum shows only bright lines, made by glowing gas that is hot and thin.

An absorption spectrum shows dark lines where cooler gas in front of a hot source takes out certain colors. And a gas absorbs exactly the same colors it emits, so the dark lines and the bright lines land in the same places. Stars show absorption spectra because their cooler outer layers sit in front of the hotter layers below.

Did you know? In 1815, Joseph von Fraunhofer counted about 600 dark lines in sunlight.

6.text:
Every Element Has a Fingerprint

A spectral fingerprint is the unique set of lines that one element makes or absorbs. No two elements share the same pattern, just like no two people share fingerprints.

Look at the slide. Hydrogen gas has its own set of lines between 400 nm and 700 nm, including the bright red H-alpha line at 656 nm. Sodium gas has a different set. Now look at the Sun's spectrum. Wherever its dark lines sit in the same places as an element's lines, that element is in the Sun.

That's how it actually happened. In 1860, Gustav Kirchhoff found sodium in the Sun by matching its lines. Same places, same element. We learned what the Sun is made of without ever touching it.

Did you know? Helium was discovered in the Sun's spectrum before anyone found it on Earth. Its name comes from helios, the Greek word for Sun.

7.text:
Motion Shifts the Lines

A Doppler shift is a change in wavelength caused by motion toward or away from us. If a star moves away, its light waves get stretched to longer wavelengths. That's a redshift. If it moves toward us, its waves get squeezed to shorter wavelengths. That's a blueshift.

On the slide, the tick shows where a line sits at rest, in a lab. A moving star's line slides away from that tick. The amount of the slide tells you the speed, using this rule: shift ÷ λ = speed ÷ c.

Try a quick example. A line that belongs at 500 nm shows up at 500.1 nm. It shifted 0.1 nm toward the red, so the star is moving away at 0.1/500 of light speed, about 60 km/s.

Did you know? Only motion straight toward or away from us causes a Doppler shift. A star moving sideways across the sky shows no shift at all.

8.text:
Hotter Glows Bluer

Think about a stove burner. As it heats, it glows dull red, then orange. Hotter things glow bluer. Stars follow the same rule.

The color where a star gives off the most light is called its peak, and there's a formula for it: peak λ = 2.9 million nm·K ÷ T, where T is the temperature in kelvins. For the Sun, the peak is about 500 nm, blue-green light. Hotter stars peak at shorter, bluer wavelengths.

The graph compares three stars. Sirius A at 9,845 K peaks far to the blue side. The Sun at 5,772 K peaks in the middle. Betelgeuse at 3,600 K peaks off toward the red. Notice that hotter stars also give off more light at every wavelength, so their curves sit higher everywhere.

Did you know? The Sun peaks in blue-green, yet it looks white. That's because it gives off plenty of every visible color, and all of them mixed together look white.

9.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Time to read some starlight. A star's hydrogen lines sit at longer wavelengths than they do in the lab. What do you know?

Is it A) it is moving away from us, B) it is very hot, C) it is made of red gas, or D) it is moving toward us? Look back at Slides 6, 7 and 8 and choose one. Be ready to explain what's wrong with each of the others.

10.text:
A Bigger Bucket for Light

A telescope's first job is to collect light. Think of it like a bucket in the rain: the wider the bucket, the more raindrops it catches. A telescope's light-gathering power depends on the area of its mirror: area = π × d² ÷ 4.

Because diameter gets squared, size matters a lot. Make a mirror twice as wide and it collects 4 times the light. Hubble's 2.4 m mirror has an area of 4.5 m², and it gathers about 120,000 times more light than your eye. On the slide, your eye is just the dot.

The Webb telescope is even bigger. Its mirror is 6.5 m across, with a collecting area of 25 m², built from 18 gold mirror segments that fit together like a honeycomb.

Did you know? Webb's mirror segments are coated with a thin layer of gold because gold reflects infrared light extremely well.

11.text:
Sharper Eyes on the Sky

A telescope's second job is to show detail. Angular resolution is the smallest angle at which two close points still look separate. Look at car headlights far away at night. From very far, the two lights blur into one. Get closer and they split into two. Good resolution means you can split them from farther away.

Two rules control resolution. A bigger mirror gives a sharper image. A longer wavelength gives a blurrier image. Radio waves are very long, so radio dishes must be huge to see sharp details.

Compare the numbers. Your eye resolves about 1 arcminute (1/60 of a degree). Ground telescopes reach a few tenths of an arcsecond, because moving air blurs the view. Hubble, above the air, reaches 0.05 arcsecond.

Did you know? One arcsecond is about the size of a US quarter seen from 5 km away.

12.text:
What Gets Through Our Air

An atmospheric window is a band of light that gets through the air all the way to the ground. Most of the spectrum doesn't make it. The grey on the chart shows light that gets absorbed.

There are two big windows. The radio window lets radio waves through, so we can use dishes on the ground. The visible window lets visible light through, which is why telescopes sit on high mountains like Maunakea, at 4,200 m.

The rest is blocked. Water vapor blocks most infrared. UV, X-rays and gamma rays are blocked too, so to see them we have to go to space. That's good news for life on Earth, since those high-energy rays are harmful, but bad news for astronomers.

Did you know? The ozone layer is what blocks most of the Sun's ultraviolet light.

13.text:
Why We Launch Telescopes

Air causes two problems: it blurs and it blocks. Launching a telescope into space solves both.

Hubble orbits about 500 km up and sees ultraviolet to near-infrared light. It has been working since 1990. Chandra studies X-rays and has been in space since 1999.

Webb is the newest of the three. It studies infrared light from 0.6 to 28.5 µm and launched in 2021. Webb sits at a spot called L2, 1.5 million km from Earth. There, a giant sunshield faces the Sun and keeps the telescope cold and dark. That matters because warm objects glow in infrared, and a warm telescope would drown out the faint light it's trying to see.

Did you know? Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.

14.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

A question about telescope design: why does Webb work in space instead of on a mountaintop?

Is it A) to get closer to the stars it studies, B) our air blocks most infrared, and space keeps it cold, C) ground telescopes cannot work at night, or D) mountains block the view of the sky? Look back at Slides 12 and 13 and pick one.

15.text:
Parallax: Measuring with Angles

Hold your thumb out at arm's length. Close one eye, then the other. Your thumb seems to jump against the background. That's parallax, and astronomers use it to measure how far away stars are.

As Earth moves around the Sun, a near star seems to shift against far background stars. Astronomers look in January and again in July, when Earth is on opposite sides of its orbit. The baseline is 1 AU, and the angle of shift is called the parallax, p.

A parsec is the distance at which a star shows a parallax of 1 arcsecond. Then d (parsecs) = 1 ÷ p (arcseconds). One parsec equals 3.26 light-years, or 206,265 AU. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star, has p = 0.768 arcsec, so it's 1.30 pc away.

Did you know? No star is within 1 parsec of us, so every star's parallax is smaller than 1 arcsecond.

16.text:
Bright, or Just Close?

Luminosity is all the power a star gives off. Apparent brightness is the light power per square meter that actually reaches us from a star. They are not the same thing, and mixing them up will fool you.

Light spreads out as it travels, covering the surface of a bigger and bigger sphere. So brightness = luminosity ÷ (4π × d²). Look at the squares on the slide. At distance d, the light covers 1 square. At 2d, it spreads over 4 squares, so it's 1/4 as bright. At 3d, it covers 9 squares, so it's 1/9 as bright.

So a dim star in the sky might be a weak star nearby, or a powerful star very far away. You can't tell until you know its distance.

Did you know? Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky mainly because it's close, only about 8.6 light-years away.

17.text:
The Sun, One AU Away

Let's test the brightness formula on a star we know. The Sun puts out 3.828 × 1026 W. Spread that over a sphere 1 AU in radius: 3.828 × 1026 W ÷ (4π × (1.496 × 1011 m)²).

The answer is 1,361 W/m², exactly the sunlight reaching Earth's distance from Deck 14. Mars, at 1.52 AU, gets only 586 W/m², less than half of what we get.

The same math works for any star. Run it backward and you get a star's luminosity: measure how bright it looks, find its distance by parallax, and multiply.

18.text:
OBAFGKM: Sorting the Stars

A spectral class is a star's letter, set by the lines in its spectrum, which track its temperature. From hottest to coolest, the classes are O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Remember them with "Oh Be A Fine Girl (Guy), Kiss Me."

O stars are over 30,000 K. B stars are 10,000 to 30,000 K, like Spica. A stars are 7,500 to 10,000 K, like Vega and Sirius A. F stars are 6,000 to 7,500 K, like Procyon A. G stars are 5,200 to 6,000 K, including the Sun, a G2 star. K stars are 3,700 to 5,200 K, like Aldebaran. M stars are 2,400 to 3,700 K, like Betelgeuse and Proxima.

Star colors run from blue at the hot end to red at the cool end. An O5 star can be as massive as 40 Suns.

Did you know? Annie Jump Cannon put these letters in order and classified about 350,000 stars, sometimes three a minute.

19.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Two stars have the same luminosity. Star Y is 3 times farther away than Star X. How bright does Y look?

Is it A) 1/3 as bright as X, B) 1/9 as bright as X, C) 3 times brighter than X, or D) just as bright as X? Look back at the squares on Slide 16 and choose carefully.

20.text:
Build the H-R Diagram

Now you get to discover one of the most important graphs in astronomy by making it yourself. This task matches standard ES.1.4.

Set up your axes. Luminosity runs up the side from 0.001 to 1,000,000, multiplying by 10 each line. Temperature runs across, with 40,000 K at the LEFT and 2,500 K at the right. Yes, hot is on the left!

Plot all 12 stars: O5 star (40,000 K, 700,000), B0 star (28,000 K, 27,000), A0 star (10,000 K, 55), F0 star (7,500 K, 5), G0 star (6,000 K, 1.4), K0 star (5,000 K, 0.35), M0 star (3,500 K, 0.05), the Sun (5,772 K, 1), Sirius A (9,845 K, 24.7), Sirius B (25,400 K, 0.024), Proxima (2,980 K, 0.0015) and Betelgeuse (3,600 K, 90,000). Luminosity is in Suns, so the Sun = 1. Color each star by its class, circle and name 3 groups, and put a star on the Sun. The data come from OpenStax, NASA and research papers.

21.text:
The H-R Diagram

The H-R diagram is a graph of stars' luminosity against their surface temperature. It's named for Hertzsprung and Russell, who each made one in the early 1900s. Hot stars are on the left, and bright stars are at the top.

About 90% of stars sit on the main sequence, a band running from hot and bright at the upper left to cool and dim at the lower right. The Sun is right in the middle of it. At the bottom right are red dwarfs, like Proxima.

Stars off the main sequence tell stories too. Cool but very bright stars at the top right must be enormous. These are giants and supergiants, like Betelgeuse. Hot but dim stars at the bottom left must be tiny. These are white dwarfs, a few percent of stars, like Sirius B.

Did you know? Sirius B is about the size of Earth, yet it holds about as much mass as the Sun.

22.text:
Weighing Stars

You can't put a star on a scale. But if a star has a partner, gravity does the weighing for you. A binary star is two stars orbiting their shared center of mass.

Kepler's third law, upgraded by Newton, gives the total mass: M1 + M2 = a³ ÷ P², with a (average separation) in AU, P (period) in years, and masses in Suns.

Try it with Sirius. One orbit takes 50.13 years, and the average separation a is 19.8 AU. So 19.8³ ÷ 50.13² = about 3.1 Suns. Watching how each star wobbles around the center of mass splits that total: Sirius A is 2.06 Suns and Sirius B is 1.02 Suns, a white dwarf. The heavier star sits closer to the center of mass, like a heavier kid sitting closer to the middle of a seesaw.

23.text:
Mass Sets the Clock

A star's mass decides how long it lives. A rough rule: lifetime ≈ mass ÷ luminosity. Mass is the fuel tank, and luminosity is how fast the star burns through it.

The catch is that bigger stars have more fuel, but they burn it much, much faster. An O5 star of 40 Suns lasts only about 1 million years on the main sequence. A B0 star of 16 Suns lasts 10 million years. An A0 star of 3.3 Suns lasts 500 million years. A G0 star of 1.1 Suns lasts 9 billion years, and the Sun about 10 billion years.

The small stars are the marathon runners. An M0 star of about 0.5 Suns lasts roughly 80 billion years, far longer than the universe has existed so far.

Did you know? Because the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, no red dwarf has ever run out of fuel yet.

24.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Time to weigh some stars yourself. Two stars 10 AU apart orbit each other every 10 years. What is their total mass?

Is it A) 1 Sun, B) 10 Suns, C) 100 Suns, or D) 1,000 Suns? Write out the formula from Slide 22, plug in the numbers, and watch your exponents.

25.text:
Exit Ticket

You've learned to read starlight like a detective. Show it with three questions.

First, a star peaks in blue light and its lines are redshifted. Name 2 things you know. Second, why do astronomers put X-ray and infrared telescopes in space? Third, where is a hot but dim star on the H-R diagram, and what kind of star is it?

When you finish, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

26.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light, using different telescopes and tools. ES.1.4: compare the life cycles of stars of different masses on the Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram, and sort low, medium (like our Sun) and high mass stars by which elements they can make and whether they become red giants or go supernova. You'll see that second part in Deck 17.

ES.1.2 is introduced here: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence such as the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law, and the cosmic microwave background. You learned the Doppler effect today, and the rest comes in Deck 19.
